Project proposal

Youjia Zhang

2026-11-18

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026

Research question

How does having a restrictive handgun waiting-period law in effect relate to the state firearm mortality rate?

The project uses two datasets already in this package. gunleg supplies the exposure, and cdcfiremort supplies the outcome. One vignette will document and construct the waiting-period exposure. A second vignette will describe firearm mortality and estimate the association.

Unit of analysis and population

The unit of analysis is the state-year. The population is the 50 states and the District of Columbia in the years for which CDC firearm mortality rates are present in cdcfiremort: 2005 and 2014 through 2024. That file has 51 locations in each of those 12 years, so the analysis set has 612 state-years. Rates for 2006 through 2013 are not in the file and will not be imputed.

cdcfiremort$Location stores the full jurisdiction name. gunleg stores the postal abbreviation in State.Postal.Abbreviation. The two files will be linked with the abbreviation crosswalk in datasets::state.abb and datasets::state.name, plus District of Columbia as DC.

Exposure

The exposure is binary. A state-year is exposed when a restrictive waiting-period law covering handguns is in effect on July 1 of that year. Handguns are specified because the RAND class mostly records handgun waiting periods, while the mortality rate is not split by firearm type. A law that becomes effective after July 1 is counted in the next mortality year, so a partial year is not coded as a full year of exposure.

The source is the RAND state firearm-law records in gunleg, restricted to Law.Class == "waiting period". This class has 111 records across 44 jurisdictions, with effective year, month, and day present on every record. Within each state, handgun records (Handguns.or.Long.Guns equal to handgun or handgun and long gun) will be ordered by effective date and read as a sequence:

  • Restrictive and Implement turns the waiting period on.
  • Restrictive and Modify leaves it on and can change the recorded length.
  • Permissive and Repeal turns it off.

Five records do not follow that pattern: a permissive implement and a permissive modify in Connecticut, both for long guns; a permissive modify for long guns in Illinois; a permissive modify for handguns in Rhode Island in 1959; and a restrictive repeal for handguns in Iowa in 2021. Long-gun-only rows are outside the primary exposure. The two atypical handgun rows will be coded from the statute text in Content, and the vignette will show the text and the resulting on or off decision. They will not be dropped quietly.

Delaware, Minnesota, Nevada, Ohio, South Carolina, Utah, and Virginia have no waiting-period record. Those states will be coded as not exposed in every analysis year. In this database, absence of a record means no waiting-period statute was catalogued, so it is an unexposed code rather than a missing value. The supersession date is blank on 65 of 111 waiting-period rows. The coding above uses the sequence of changes, so a blank supersession date will not be imputed and will not, by itself, mark a law as missing.

A sensitivity analysis will repeat the construction with long-gun waiting periods included, so the exposure is on when either a handgun or a long-gun waiting period is in effect on July 1.

Outcome

The outcome is Death.Rate in cdcfiremort, a continuous firearm mortality rate for each state-year. The rate is present for all 612 rows. Deaths. is the corresponding count and will be summarized, but it is not the outcome, because states differ in population size. The rate combines firearm deaths and is not limited to homicide.

Confounders

These adjustment variables are specified from the structure of the question, before estimating the association.

The primary model will include state indicators and year indicators. State indicators absorb stable differences across states, including long-run differences in gun ownership, urbanicity, and economic conditions. Year indicators absorb shocks shared by all states in a given year, including the mortality increase around 2020.

Age composition, poverty, firearm ownership, and other firearm laws passed in the same year are not in these two files. They remain unmeasured confounders. As one pre-specified sensitivity analysis, a restrictive permit-to-purchase law will be coded from gunleg with the same July 1 rule and added as a covariate, because that policy is often adopted together with a waiting period. No other law class will be added after seeing the waiting-period estimate.

Planned summaries and report

The gun-law vignette will give the RAND provenance, the count of waiting-period records, and a table of which states are exposed in each analysis year. The mortality vignette will give the CDC provenance, the distribution of Death.Rate overall and by exposure, and the state-and-year-adjusted association, with a confidence interval and standard errors clustered by state. The written conclusion will be limited to this state-year comparison. It will state the gap from 2006 to 2013, the difference between a handgun law and an all-firearm death rate, and the confounders that these files do not measure.
